newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST- Slight tapering seen in Mar US trade gap.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST- Slight tapering seen in Mar US trade gap.

text.p: Continued strength in exports and flat-to-lower imports probably led to a slight narrowing in the U.S. trade deficit during March, economists said on Monday.

They cited recent data indicating substantial declines in import prices, a recent buildup of importer inventories and lower imported oil prices as well as better export figures in recent months from the National Association of Purchasing Management.
Higher Japanese consumer spending in anticipation of the country's consumption tax hike, which took effect at the beginning of April, also may have helped exports in March, forecasters said.
The Commerce Department will release the trade data at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Wednesday, May 21.

"I'm looking for a deficit of $10.3 billion," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at REFCO Group Ltd in Chicago. 'You will probably see still relatively strong exports and slightly diminished imports."

Malpede's forecast comes in precisely in line with Wall Street consensus expectations for a $10.3 billion March shortfall. Last month, after announcing that its initial trade report contained reporting errors for oil imports, the Commerce Department revised the February deficit to $10.4 billion.
In that report, imports showed a 1.1 percent rise to $83.88 billion while exports jumped 4.0 percent to $73.46 billion.

John Rothfield, international economist at NationsBanc-CRT in Chicago said the March trade assumption the Commerce Department used in calculating its preliminary estimate of first quarter gross domestic product could come close to the actual number.
"We think the government has a good chance of achieving the $9.0 to $9.5 billion deficit primarily because we think imports were held down again in March," he said.

Rothfield also expects improvements in Canadian domestic demand to lead to better U.S. exports to its NAFTA neighbor. With the rest of the world, however, he said there will be a great deal of variation in the months ahead.

"We expect the deficit to rise with Japan and another fairly gloomy development is that demand in Mexico seems to have slowed a little," he said. "But we do expect a fairly rapid improvement with Europe and Canada and that should more than outweigh the deterioration with Japan and Mexico."

Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp was less optimistic about the prospects for a narrowing gap in March, predicting further gains in imports and a drop-off in exports after last month's heady gain.

"I'm looking for a deficit of $12.25 billion," Liro said. "I have imports rising yet again based on the very heavy inflow of inventories in the first quarter including March ... and conversely I have exports declining slightly after being up significantly in February."
Liro said the risk to his forecast was weaker overall imports due to a decline in oil imports.
Economists predicted greater downside than upside potential for the dollar -- which has weakened roughly 10 percent against the yen in recent weeks -- from the report.

They also said that the impact of a stronger dollar, which was near its recent four-and-a-half year peak against the yen and three-year highs versus the mark in March, would have a greater effect on trade figures later in the year.
